extracted.intended_audience: students, teachers, and scholars of communication/media studies and cultural studies (including journalists and researchers interested in theory and history of mass media)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for studying, evaluating, and producing scholarship in communication and media studies from a cultural/ritual perspective—emphasizing historical, interpretive, and democratic dimensions rather than narrow behaviorist or technocratic approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication is not merely transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication is not merely the transmission of information; it also includes the drawing-together of a people that is culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broaden analysis beyond 'messages' and flows: study how communication builds community and cultural cohesion. Examine symbolic meanings and communal effects, not just message delivery or sender motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritual (culturalist) view of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: A ritual view of communication is directed not toward the extension of messages in space but toward the maintenance of society in time; not the act of imparting information but the representation of shared beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate practices (ceremonies, journalism as stylized speech, oral traditions) for how they sustain communal meaning and continuity. Treat media as part of cultural ritual, assessing their role in preserving shared commitments and memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission view of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The transmission view treats communication as the extension of messages across geography for purposes such as control—the archetypal case being extending information across space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the transmission model's strengths (e.g., logistics, markets, speed of information) but not as the sole analytic frame. Identify when scholarship or policy is over-dominated by this model (e.g., effects research that reduces communication to signal propagation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate ritual and transmission views
rubrics_metrics.description: A fully developed understanding of communication involves both a ritual and a transmission view; modern societies require both forms to be at play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess media phenomena for both their spatial/functional effects and their temporal/cultural functions—how they move messages and how they sustain communal meanings. Avoid analyses that privilege only one perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center mass media as a site for social theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural studies 'centers the mass media as a site (not a subject or a discipline) on which to engage the general question of social theory: How is social life produced and reproduced?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use media and mass communication as the locus to ask broader social-theoretical questions about social reproduction, identity, and institutions rather than treating media merely as an applied subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask technology-focused historical questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Students of communications should ask: how do changes in forms of communications technology affect the constructions placed on experience? How does such technology change the forms of community in which experience is apprehended and expressed? What is thought about, thought with, and to whom is it expressed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame research questions that probe technologies' effects on: (a) what people think about, (b) the conceptual tools they use (symbols), and (c) the audiences/communities that receive expression. Use historical cases (telegraph, radio, Internet) as comparative data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor historically and theoretically informed inquiry over scientistic determinism
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace the search for deterministic laws of behavior and reliance on 'scientistic' behaviorist methods with historically- and theoretically-grounded interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize historical context, theoretical nuance, and interpretive depth. Use empirical methods when appropriate but resist reduction to rules that ignore meaning, contingency, and cultural specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reduce culture to ideology or class conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural studies should not reduce culture to ideology, social conflict to class conflict, consent to compliance, action to reproduction, or communication to coercion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid single-factor reductionisms. Maintain pluralist analyses that can represent mythic, ritual, anthropological, and ideological dimensions together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlarge the human conversation (normative aim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarship should aim 'to enlarge the human conversation by comprehending what others are saying.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess research and practice by whether they deepen mutual understanding, bring diverse voices into dialogue, and enrich public discourse—rather than merely measuring effects or producing interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value oral communication and its democratic role
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic politics are born in the domain of oral exchange—a public sphere of face-to-face discussion; oral exchange supports memory, argument, and resistance to elite monopolies of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating media forms, consider their capacity to approximate or sustain oral-discursive qualities (dialogue, deliberation, memory) and their implications for democratic participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider media's bias to space or time (Innis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication technologies promote a 'bias' either to space (light, portable media) or to time (time-binding media promoting permanence); technologies shape organization of societies accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze technologies for whether they privilege spatial expansion/control or temporal continuity/anchoring. Use this bias to interpret cultural shifts (e.g., telegraph/railroads → space-binding; oral manuscripts → time-binding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware the 'technological sublime' and hype
rubrics_metrics.description: The rhetoric of the technological sublime (elite-inspired hype) can deflect attention from social costs; such rhetoric may operate as false consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate technological claims critically: interrogate promises of progress or utopia, assess social costs and unequal effects, and separate marketing rhetoric from material consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate empirical 'effects' research when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: While criticizing the limits of administrative/effects research, do not discard its contributions—incorporate its results where appropriate into historical and interpretive accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quantitative/experimental findings as one input among many; synthesize empirical evidence with hermeneutic and historical methods rather than privileging it exclusively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarship should judge and shape social practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The social scientist is not only an analyst but bears responsibility to judge and to shape practices—scholarship is both diagnostic and normative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess work for its reflexive ethical stance: explicit normative commitments (e.g., democratic renewal) are valid research outcomes. Make clear the values informing analyses and proposed interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt 'useful ethnocentrism' / nation-contextualization
rubrics_metrics.description: Care for the nation-specific contours of cultural formation—read cultures often within the boundaries of the nation-state (a 'useful ethnocentrism').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground studies in particular national histories and political economies rather than assuming universal trajectories; contextualize technologies/media within national institutions and narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat symbols as productive—not merely representational—of reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Reality is brought into existence, produced by communication—by the construction, apprehension, and utilization of symbolic forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse how symbolic systems (language, ritual, media forms) actively construct social realities, identities, and institutions; attend to performative and constitutive effects of media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer interpretive methods (hermeneutics, ethnography, semiotics) for cultural meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural approach privileges understanding meaning—ethnography, hermeneutics, semiotic analysis—over exclusively behaviorist/experimental techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use qualitative methods to recover meanings, rituals, and practices; combine with archival and historical methods to trace change over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to continuity and change between oral and literate traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern societies are shaped by tensions between oral and written traditions; media transformations create strains on communal foundations that require study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating media change, analyze how literacy, print, telegraph, broadcast, and digital media reorganize memory, attention, and community. Examine what is preserved and what is lost in transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze effects of standardization, centralization, and monopolies
rubrics_metrics.description: Media and communication systems (e.g., telegraph, standard time) can produce centralization, monopolies of knowledge, and standardizing effects that reorganize communities and power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate institutional and infrastructural consequences (standard time, centralized distribution, corporate control) alongside cultural meanings; assess implications for access, plurality, and democratic deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote democratic virtues as a metric of quality
rubrics_metrics.description: A measure of a theory's or research program's worth is the degree to which it encourages democratic practices and preserves civic virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge scholarship and media practices by their contribution to informed public deliberation, inclusiveness, and empowerment—not only by predictive power or technical efficiency.
